scenes.label: The printer that went quiet
scenes.narration: [dramatically] Hackers tried to steal almost a billion dollars, and a printer hid it. [short pause] [quietly] Friday morning, February 5, 2016. Dhaka, Bangladesh. A senior officer named Zubair Bin Huda walks over to a printer. It sits inside the country's central bank. Every morning, it prints a paper record of the bank's money transfers abroad. But today, the tray is empty. He tries to print the records by hand. Nothing works. He doesn't worry much. It has acted up before. [ominously] But this time, the money is already on the move.

scenes.label: A bank for a whole country
scenes.narration: [calmly] So what is Bangladesh Bank? It isn't a normal bank. It's the central bank of Bangladesh. Think of it as the country's version of the Federal Reserve. It keeps a big part of the nation's savings in US dollars. Much of that money sits in one account. That account is in New York, at the Federal Reserve Bank. The country uses this money to pay for things it buys from other countries. [serious] So whoever came for it wasn't just robbing a bank. They were robbing a nation.

visuals.query: Federal Reserve Bank of New York building

visuals.at: things it buys from other countries

scenes.label: A job application
scenes.narration: [curious] To see how it happened, we have to go back a full year. It's January 2015. A few people at Bangladesh Bank get an email. It's from a job seeker named Rasel Ahlam. He's polite. He says his resume is attached. But Rasel Ahlam wasn't real. The email was a trap. Opening the file could quietly let strangers into the computer. Investigators say at least one person opened it. [whispers] And that one click opened the door.

visuals.at: A few people at Bangladesh Bank
at least one person opened it
that one click opened the door

scenes.label: The thieves who waited
scenes.narration: [slowly] Then the hackers did something strange for thieves. They waited. For months, they crept quietly through the bank's computers. They were looking for one thing. It's called SWIFT. SWIFT is like a super-safe email system for banks. Banks use it to tell each other where to send money. A message from a central bank carries a lot of trust. So if you could send those messages yourself… [whispers] you wouldn't need to break into a vault. You could just ask.

visuals.at: crept quietly through the bank's computers

visuals.text: SWIFT: how banks message each other

scenes.label: Four quiet accounts in Manila
scenes.narration: [cautiously] Meanwhile, someone was getting the escape route ready. This was in Manila, the capital of the Philippines. In May 2015, four bank accounts were opened there. They were at a bank called RCBC, at its branch on Jupiter Street. News reports say they were opened with fake driver's licenses. Each account got just $500. Then nothing happened. For nine months, the accounts just sat there. Empty. Quiet. Waiting.

visuals.query: Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation RCBC Plaza Makati

scenes.label: The perfect weekend
scenes.narration: [serious] Next, the hackers picked their moment. And they picked it well. In Bangladesh, the weekend is Friday and Saturday. In New York, it's Saturday and Sunday. And that Monday, February 8, was Lunar New Year. That's a holiday in the Philippines. Put it all together. For several days, the three places would never be at work at the same time. So if something went wrong, who would answer the phone?

visuals.text: Fri to Mon: nobody at work

scenes.label: Nearly a billion dollars
scenes.narration: [dramatically] Thursday night, February 4, Dhaka time. The bank had closed for the weekend. That's when the hackers struck. Using the bank's own SWIFT system, they sent 35 payment orders to New York. Together, the orders asked for about $951 million. That's almost all the money in the account. To the Fed, the messages looked real. And back in Dhaka, the hackers had secretly changed the software that ran that printer. [whispers] So nobody would see a thing.

visuals.at: the software that ran that printer

scenes.label: Saved by a street name
scenes.narration: [curious] Then something strange happened. The New York Fed's system flagged many of the orders. Why? According to Reuters, part of the reason was one word. Jupiter. Remember the branch on Jupiter Street? Jupiter was also the name of a ship and a shipping company on a US blacklist. The two had nothing to do with each other. It was pure luck. But that one word slowed everything down. Most of the orders were never paid.

visuals.query: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Liberty Street

scenes.label: One typo, $20 million
scenes.narration: [serious] Most. But not all. Five orders got through. One of them sent $20 million to Sri Lanka. It was meant for a group called the Shalika Foundation. But the hackers spelled it wrong. They typed Fandation. [short pause] A bank in the middle, Deutsche Bank, spotted the typo and asked questions. That money was stopped. [exhales] The other four payments went to Manila. That's $81 million, landing in those quiet accounts on Jupiter Street.

visuals.at: a group called the Shalika Foundation

scenes.label: Nobody picks up
scenes.narration: [nervous] Back in Dhaka, staff fought with the printer for more than a day. On Saturday, February 6, they finally printed the records by hand. And then they saw it. The New York Fed had been asking about dozens of payment orders. Orders the bank never meant to send. [urgently] The bank sent a message. Our system has been hacked. Please stop all payment instructions immediately. They emailed. They called. They faxed. But it was the weekend in New York. And nobody answered.

scenes.label: A message one day late
scenes.narration: [serious] Monday came. It was Lunar New Year in the Philippines. Bangladesh Bank sent an urgent message to RCBC. Stop the payments. Freeze the money. But the message didn't arrive until the next day. By then, it was too late. The money had been moved between accounts and turned into Philippine pesos. Much of it was taken out as cash. About $58 million had already left the Jupiter Street branch. [sighs] The trail was going cold.

visuals.at: Lunar New Year in the Philippines
didn't arrive until the next day
had already left the Jupiter Street branch

scenes.label: Lost in the casinos
scenes.narration: [curious] So where did the money go? A lot of it went to casinos. Reports say about $50 million went to accounts linked to two Manila casinos. Why casinos? Back then, the Philippines' law against money laundering didn't cover them. Money laundering means hiding where dirty money came from. Once the cash hit the gambling tables, it was almost impossible to follow. Another $31 million reportedly went to a Chinese man named Xu Weikang. Reports say he left on a private plane. He hasn't been seen since.

visuals.at: hiding where dirty money came from

scenes.label: So who did it?
scenes.narration: [serious] For two years, one big question hung in the air. Who did this? Then, on September 6, 2018, the US Justice Department gave its answer. It charged a North Korean computer programmer named Park Jin Hyok. Prosecutors say he worked for a hacking team backed by North Korea's government. Security experts call that group Lazarus. He has never been arrested. Today, he's on the FBI's wanted list. And the charges have never been tested in court.

visuals.query: Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice Building

scenes.label: A clue from Hollywood
scenes.narration: [curious] How did the FBI link him to this? Through clues hidden in the hacking tools. The FBI says tools used in different attacks shared the same hidden fingerprints. Some of those fingerprints also showed up in the 2014 hack of the movie studio Sony Pictures. Prosecutors say the same group did both. And Bangladesh was just one target. The Justice Department says that from 2015 to 2018, the group tried to steal at least $1 billion from banks around the world.

visuals.at: How did the FBI link him
clues hidden in the hacking tools

scenes.label: Who paid the price
scenes.narration: [reflective] The fallout was fast. In March 2016, the head of Bangladesh Bank, Governor Atiur Rahman, quit his job. In Manila, the branch manager on Jupiter Street was charged. Her name was Maia Santos Deguito. In January 2019, a court found her guilty of money laundering and sentenced her to prison. In 2023, a higher court agreed. Bangladesh Bank also sued RCBC in a New York court. [sighs] That legal fight dragged on for years.

visuals.query: New York County Supreme Court building

scenes.label: A billion asked, $81M gone
scenes.narration: [slowly] So let's add it up. The hackers asked for nearly $1 billion. They got away with $81 million. Only about $15 million of it ever came back. They weren't stopped by some genius security system. They were stopped by a street name, a spelling mistake and a lot of luck. After this, banks everywhere worked harder to guard their SWIFT systems. [softly] One of the biggest cyber heists ever didn't start with a gun. It started with a fake job email… and a printer nobody worried about. If you like stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

facts.claim: Hackers sent 35 fraudulent SWIFT payment orders to the New York Fed on February 4, 2016, requesting about $951 million
Five payments worth $101 million were paid; $20 million to Sri Lanka was reversed, $81 million went to four accounts in the Philippines
Jupiter in the Manila bank address matched a US-sanctioned tanker/shipping company name, raising alarms at the Fed
Bangladesh Bank's emergency email: 'Our system has been hacked. Please stop all payment (debit) instructions immediately.'
The Fed said the instructions were fully authenticated by the SWIFT messaging system
Printer fault on February 5; joint director Zubair bin Huda: glitches happened before, thought it was a common problem
The printer held the paper record of transfers; hackers tampered with its software
January 2015 phishing email from fake job applicant 'Rasel Ahlam'
Four RCBC Jupiter Street accounts opened May 2015 with fake driver's licenses and $500 deposits
Bangladesh weekend Friday-Saturday; Lunar New Year Monday February 8, 2016
$20 million to 'Shalika Fandation' blocked after Deutsche Bank questioned the misspelling
About $50 million went to Solaire and Midas casinos; $31 million to Xu Weikang who left by private plane; casinos not covered by AML law
DOJ complaint against Park Jin Hyok filed June 8, 2018, unsealed September 6, 2018; conspiracy to commit computer fraud and wire fraud
Shared malware data table linked Sony Pictures attack and bank intrusions; group attempted thefts of at least $1 billion 2015-2018
Governor Atiur Rahman resigned in March 2016
Maia Deguito convicted on eight counts of money laundering by Makati RTC in January 2019, 4 to 7 years
Court of Appeals upheld Deguito's conviction in 2023
Bangladesh Bank sued RCBC in New York; litigation ongoing for years

Morning of Friday Feb 5, 2016, joint director Zubair Bin Huda found the printer tray empty and could not print SWIFT confirmations manually; colleagues worked more than 24 hours; on Saturday Feb 6 receipts printed manually showed New York Fed queries about dozens of payment orders

On Monday Feb 8 (Lunar New Year holiday in the Philippines) Bangladesh Bank asked RCBC via SWIFT to stop payments and freeze funds; the message reached RCBC a day later, by which time about $58 million had been withdrawn from the Jupiter Street branch
Funds were converted to Philippine pesos and moved between accounts; about $15 million of the $81 million sent to the Philippines has been recovered
Park Jin Hyok is listed on the FBI's Cyber's Most Wanted list
Bangladesh Bank staff tried to reach the New York Fed by email, phone and fax over the US weekend without response

seo.youtube_title: How Bangladesh Bank Was Hacked: The $1 Billion Heist Saved by a Typo
seo.youtube_description:
How was Bangladesh Bank hacked? This is the true story of the 2016 cyber heist where hackers tried to steal almost $1 billion from the New York Fed.
A fake job email, a broken printer and a long holiday weekend. The Bangladesh Bank heist, explained in plain English.

In February 2016, hackers used Bangladesh Bank's own SWIFT system to send 35 fake payment orders to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. They asked for about $951 million. A street name that matched a US blacklist and a simple spelling mistake stopped most of it. But $81 million still reached bank accounts in the Philippines and disappeared into casinos.

Two years later, the US Justice Department charged a North Korean programmer, Park Jin Hyok. Prosecutors say he was part of the government-backed hacking team known as Lazarus, the same group they blame for the Sony Pictures hack.
